::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning Objectives

* Understand what is meant by **differential localisation** and why it is
  studied with dynamic (multi-condition) correlation profiling experiments
* Know the difference between the **BANDLE** and **SANDLE** approaches to
  differential localisation, and when you might choose each
* Run the **marker-based** and **marker-free** SANDLE tests on a replicated
  two-condition LOPIT experiment
* Combine and threshold the results to produce a ranked list of candidate
  differentially localised proteins
* Describe where candidates move, including movements to and from proteins
  with no confident niche assignment (`"unknown"`)
* Visualise candidate movers using protein profiles, PCA spatial maps and
  alluvial plots, and critically assess the evidence for movement
:::

```{r, include=FALSE}
library("MSnbase")
library("pRoloc")
library("robustbase")
library("glasso")
library("mvtnorm")
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
library("here")
```

## From static maps to dynamic experiments

In the previous lessons we generated a **static** spatial map: for a single
condition we used marker proteins and machine learning to predict where each
protein resides in the cell. Whilst the steady-state localisation of proteins
can provide vital information about function, these localisations are specific
to the system of interest under the study conditions. Given the functional
importance of protein localisation, the question naturally extends from
profiling the spatial proteome of a single condition to
**comparing the spatial proteome between conditions**. Correlation profiling
methods have been widely applied to study protein dynamics in response to drugs,
stress, signalling and differentiation [@Itzhak2016; @Orre2019; @Mulvey2021;
@Christopher2025].

We say a protein is **differentially localised** if it is assigned to a
different subcellular location (or *niche*) in one condition compared with
another. Discovering these proteins is the main goal of a dynamic spatial
proteomics experiment.

:::{.callout-note}
#### What does "differentially localised" mean in practice?
A correlation profiling experiment measures the distribution of each protein
across a set of biochemical fractions. If a protein relocates, its
distribution across the fractions (its **profile**) changes shape so that it
now looks like the profile of a different organelle. A change in the *amount*
of a protein (expression) without a change in profile shape is not
differential localisation.
:::

## The use-case data: insulin-stimulated adipocytes

In this lesson we use a dynamic LOPIT dataset of 3T3-L1 adipocytes
[@Conway2026]. Cells were analysed in two conditions:

1. **basal** (unstimulated)
2. **insulin-stimulated**

Each condition was profiled in **three biological replicates**, and each
replicate was fractionated into **10 fractions** and quantified with TMT
10-plex labelling. Replicate 1 of the basal condition was processed alongside
replicate 1 of the insulin condition, and so on, which means the replicates are
**paired**.

Insulin signalling in adipocytes is a classic example of regulated protein
trafficking. The best-known example is the glucose transporter GLUT4 (Slc2a4),
which is held in intracellular storage vesicles under basal conditions and is
rapidly delivered to the plasma membrane in response to insulin, allowing the
cell to take up glucose. We should therefore expect to see some proteins
moving in this dataset.

## BANDLE and SANDLE

In the workflow paper accompanying this course [@Hutchings2025] we used
**BANDLE** (Bayesian ANalysis of Differential Localisation Experiments)
[@Crook2022] to find differentially localised proteins. BANDLE is a fully
Bayesian model,  it uses Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample from the
posterior distribution of its parameters, and it outputs a differential
localisation probability for each protein. It is powerful, but it requires the
user to set priors, run several long MCMC chains (typically on a
high-performance computing cluster), and check that the chains have converged
before the results can be used.

**SANDLE** (Statistical ANalysis of Differential Localisation Experiments)
[@Crook2026] was designed to answer the same question quickly and robustly,
and to handle more complex experimental designs.

| | BANDLE | SANDLE |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Fully Bayesian (Gaussian processes + MCMC) | Robust mixture model + regression test |
| Run time | Minutes to hours; HPC often needed | Seconds on a laptop |
| Priors to set | Yes | No |
| Convergence checks | Yes | No |
| Needs markers | Yes | Marker-based test yes, marker-free test no |
| Paired / multi-condition designs | Pairwise comparisons only | Supported |
| Output | DL probability + localisation predictions | DL probability + p-value / FDR |

SANDLE combines two complementary tests:

1. **Marker-based test.** Using the markers, SANDLE models each subcellular
   niche in each replicate with a robust multivariate *t*-distribution. The
   centre and spread of each niche are estimated with the minimum covariance
   determinant (MCD), which is insensitive to outlying markers, and graphical
   lasso regularisation keeps the estimates stable when a niche has few
   markers. Every protein then gets a probability of belonging to each niche,
   in each condition. The **differential localisation (DL) probability**
   compares these probabilities between the conditions: it is the probability
   that the niche a protein belongs to in the basal condition differs from the
   niche it belongs to in the insulin condition. In other words, it reflects
   our confidence that a protein changes compartmental identity [@Crook2026].
   The test is called marker-based because it uses the markers to build its
   model of the niches.

2. **Marker-free test.** This test ignores markers and organelles altogether.
   It asks whether the *shape* of a protein's profile changes between the
   conditions by more than we would expect from replicate-to-replicate noise.
   The result is a classical **p-value**, corrected for multiple testing to
   give a **false discovery rate (FDR)**.

The two tests capture different kinds of evidence: "is the protein assigned to a
different organelle?" and "has its profile changed?". Together they give each
protein a DL probability and an FDR, which you can use to rank and explore
candidates. There is no single correct way to decide which proteins are
differentially localised, you might threshold on the DL probability, on the FDR,
on both, or on either, and the thresholds themselves are a choice. Requiring
both tests to pass gives a short, conservative list with few false positives
[@Crook2026], while thresholding on either test, or using looser thresholds,
gives a longer list for exploration. The right choice depends on your biological
question and on what you plan to do with the candidates next.


## SANDLE setup

SANDLE has not yet been released as an R package. For this course, all the
functions you need are in one script, `sandle_functions.R`, which we load with
`source()`. You will also need the `MSnbase` and `pRoloc` packages from
Bioconductor, which we used in previous lessons.

```{r}
source("code/sandle_functions.R")
```

The script provides the following functions:

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `split_by_replicate()` | Splits an `MSnSet` into a list of `MSnSet`s, one per replicate |
| `sandle_markers()` | Marker-based test, returns a DL probability per protein |
| `sandle_marker_free()` | Marker-free test, returns p-values and FDR per protein |
| `combine_results()` | Joins the two result tables by protein |
| `plot_marker_profiles()` | Quality control plot of the fitted organelle profiles |
| `plot_dl_results()` | Plots DL probability against FDR |
| `plot_protein_profiles()` | Plots the profiles of chosen proteins in both conditions |

## Importing the data

### Why `readMSnSet2()`?

In the previous lessons we started from PSM-level output, processed it in a
`QFeatures` object, aggregated it to protein level and then coerced the
protein-level sets into `MSnSet`s with `as(..., "MSnSet")`, so that we could
use `pRoloc`.

In practice, you will often be given data that has *already* been processed
to protein level: a table exported from Proteome Discoverer or MaxQuant, the
output of a collaborator's pipeline, or a supplementary table from a paper.
This is the case for the adipocyte data. There is no PSM-level data to
process, so we don't need `QFeatures`. Instead, we can read the table straight
into an `MSnSet` with the `readMSnSet2()` function from `MSnbase`. The end
result is the same kind of object we created by coercion, and everything we
learnt about `pRoloc` applies to it.

:::{.callout-note}
#### Reminder: the three parts of an `MSnSet`
An `MSnSet` stores three linked tables:

* `exprs()`: the quantitative data, with proteins in rows and samples (here,
  fractions) in columns
* `fData()`: the **feature data**, with one row per protein and any
  information about it, such as marker annotation
* `pData()`: the **sample data**, with one row per column of `exprs()`, such
  as the TMT tag, condition and replicate

`readMSnSet2()` builds the first two from a single spreadsheet. We add the
third ourselves.
:::

### Look at the file first

Before importing, it is good practice to look at the column names so we know
which columns hold the quantitation and which hold the protein information.
We read just the header row of the basal file using the `getEcols()` function.

```{r}
getEcols(f = "data/adipocytes2025_basal.csv", split = ",")
```

The first column, `Accession`, holds the UniProt accessions. Columns 2 to 31
hold the quantitation: 10 TMT channels (the fractions) for each of the three
replicates, named by tag, condition and replicate. All the remaining columns
are information about each protein, including the `markers` column.

### Read the data into an `MSnSet`

`readMSnSet2()` needs to be told two things:

* `ecol`: which columns hold the quantitative data. Here this is columns
  `2:31`. These become the `exprs()` matrix.
* `fnames`: which column holds the protein names. Here this is `"Accession"`.
  These become the row names (`featureNames()`) of the `MSnSet`.

All other columns go into the feature data. Any further arguments are passed
on to `read.csv()`. We set `check.names = FALSE` so that R keeps the column
names exactly as they are in the file. Without it, R would add an "X" to the
start of names that begin with a number, such as `26_Basal_rep1`.


```{r}
basal   <- readMSnSet2("data/adipocytes2025_basal.csv",
                       ecol = 2:31,
                       fnames = "Accession",
                       check.names = FALSE)

insulin <- readMSnSet2("data/adipocytes2025_insulin.csv",
                       ecol = 2:31,
                       fnames = "Accession",
                       check.names = FALSE)
```

Let's check that everything went where we expected:

```{r}
dim(basal)                 # proteins x quantitative columns
head(exprs(basal)[, 1:5])  # quantitation
head(fvarLabels(basal))    # feature data column names
```

### Add the sample data

The `readMSnSet2()` function only reads the protein table, so the sample data is
empty. We add it from a second, small file that describes each of the 30
quantitative columns: its TMT tag, condition (`Treatment`) and `Replicate`. The
row names of this table must match the column names of `exprs()`.

```{r}
pData(basal)   <- read.csv("data/sampleInfo_basal.csv",   row.names = 1)
pData(insulin) <- read.csv("data/sampleInfo_insulin.csv", row.names = 1)

pData(basal)
```

Our `MSnSet`s are now complete:

```{r}
basal
```

```{r}
insulin
```


### Splitting the data by replicate

SANDLE needs one `MSnSet` per replicate. The `split_by_replicate()` function
splits the data using the `Replicate` column of the sample data.

```{r}
control <- split_by_replicate(basal, rep_col = "Replicate")    # basal
treated <- split_by_replicate(insulin, rep_col = "Replicate")  # insulin

length(control)
length(treated)

control[[1]]
```

:::{.callout-warning}
#### Replicate order matters
The replicates must be in the same order in both lists, so `control[[1]]` and
`treated[[1]]` are the replicates that were processed together, and so on.
The marker-free test compares each insulin replicate with its matching basal
replicate, so it relies on this.
:::

The marker proteins are stored in the `markers` column of the feature data.
As in BANDLE, **the same marker list must be used for all replicates of all
conditions**. The markers are assumed not to move between conditions.

```{r}
table(fData(control[[1]])$markers)
```

## Exploring the data

Differential localisation analysis relies on the same thing as static
localisation: well-resolved subcellular niches. Before we run any test we
should therefore look at each replicate. Here we use `plot2D()` to plot the
first two principal components of each replicate, coloured by marker.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10
par(mfrow = c(3, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:3) plot2D(control[[i]], fcol = "markers", main = paste("Basal, rep", i))
for (i in 1:3) plot2D(treated[[i]], fcol = "markers", main = paste("Insulin, rep", i))
addLegend(control[[1]], fcol = "markers", where = "other", ncol = 2)
```

We see clear, separated clusters for most organelles and a similar overall
picture in every replicate of both conditions. Note that each PCA is computed
separately, so the plots may be rotated or mirrored relative to each other.
What matters is the relative position of the clusters.

:::{.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge 1: Assessing resolution
{{< level 2 >}}

In a previous lesson we used `QSep()` to quantify how well the subcellular
niches are separated. Calculate the QSep scores for replicate 1 of the basal
and insulin data and plot them. Are the organelles equally well resolved in
both conditions? Which niches are least well separated?

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}

```{r}
qs_basal   <- QSep(control[[1]], fcol = "markers")
qs_insulin <- QSep(treated[[1]], fcol = "markers")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(qs_basal, main = "Basal, rep 1")
plot(qs_insulin, main = "Insulin, rep 1")
```

The resolution is similar in both conditions. This is reassuring: if one
condition were much less well resolved, we would expect more apparent
"movement" simply because proteins are assigned less confidently.

:::
:::

## Marker-based SANDLE

The marker-based test is a single function call. `sandle_markers()` fits a
robust *t*-distribution to every niche in every replicate, computes the niche
probabilities for every protein, and combines them into a DL probability. We
pass the two lists of replicates and the name of the marker column.

The robust fitting step uses random subsampling, so we set a seed to make the
result reproducible.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(1)
marker_res <- sandle_markers(control, treated, fcol = "markers")
head(marker_res)
```

The output is a `data.frame` with one row per protein:

* `dl_prob`: the differential localisation probability
* `is_marker`: whether the protein is a marker. Markers are given a DL
  probability of 0 because they are assumed not to move
* `niche_control` and `niche_treated`: the most probable niche in each
  condition, averaged over replicates. These tell us *where from* and *where
  to*
* `prob_control` and `prob_treated`: the probability of that most probable
  niche. We will use these later to decide whether a niche assignment is
  confident

As a quality control step, we look at the fitted profile (mean ± 1 standard
deviation) of each niche in one replicate. Each organelle should have a
distinct and reasonably tight profile.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
plot_marker_profiles(marker_res, replicate = 1)
```

:::{.callout-note}
#### How the DL probability is computed
For each protein, SANDLE averages the niche probabilities over the replicates
of each condition. The DL probability is then the probability that a niche
drawn for the basal condition differs from a niche drawn for the insulin
condition, $1 - \sum_k p_k^{\text{basal}}\, p_k^{\text{insulin}}$. A protein
confidently assigned to the same niche in both conditions scores close to 0;
a protein confidently assigned to different niches scores close to 1.

Because the DL probability uses the full set of niche probabilities, and not
just the single most probable niche, it responds to any change in how a
protein's probability is spread across the niches. This includes a protein
that leaves an organelle and ends up between several, or one that becomes
partly associated with a second niche. What it does not see are changes in
profile that leave the niche probabilities unchanged, for example a shift
within a single niche. Note also that a protein that is uncertain in both
conditions gets a non-zero DL probability even if it does not move, because
two uncertain niche draws can differ by chance.
:::

## Marker-free SANDLE

The marker-free test is also a single call. It needs no markers and no model
fitting, so it takes well under a second.

```{r}
free_res <- sandle_marker_free(control, treated)
head(free_res)
```

For each protein we get:

* `p_value` and `fdr`: the p-value from the F-test and the Benjamini-Hochberg
  adjusted FDR
* `neg_log10_fdr`: $-\log_{10}(\text{FDR})$, convenient for plotting
* `F_stat`: the F statistic
* `RSS_diff`: the difference in residual sum of squares between the two
  models, an **effect size** describing how much the profile changes

## Combining the two tests

We now join the two result tables by protein.

```{r}
results <- combine_results(marker_res, free_res)
head(results)
```

To see how the two tests relate, we plot the DL probability on the x-axis
against $-\log_{10}(\text{FDR})$ on the y-axis. The dashed lines show the
thresholds we will use: DL probability > 0.9 and FDR < 0.1. Proteins in the
top-right corner are supported by **both** tests. Point size shows the effect
size (`RSS_diff`).

We also highlight in red some proteins that were reported to move after
insulin stimulation in the original study [@Conway2026].

```{r}
known_movers <- c("P14142", "Q8C129", "P40336", "P81122", "Q05512",
                  "Q9JLN9", "Q8CFH6", "P61460", "Q8C0M0", "A2A9C3")
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
plot_dl_results(results, prob_cut = 0.9, fdr_cut = 0.1, highlight = known_movers)
```

How many candidates do we get with each criterion?

```{r}
c(marker_based = sum(results$dl_prob > 0.9),
  marker_free  = sum(results$fdr < 0.1),
  both         = sum(results$dl_prob > 0.9 & results$fdr < 0.1),
  either       = sum(results$dl_prob > 0.9 | results$fdr < 0.1))
```

The marker-free test flags many more proteins than the marker-based test.
This is expected, because the two tests ask different questions. The
marker-free test detects *any* consistent change in profile shape, including
small shifts within the same organelle. The marker-based test asks whether the
protein's membership of the niches defined by the markers has changed, so a
change in profile only counts if it changes which niches the protein is
likely to belong to. How you combine them is up to you. Here we take the
conservative option and require both, which gives a short list to start
exploring. For comparison, @Crook2026 required a DL probability of at least
0.8 and an FDR below 0.05 for this dataset. Challenge 2 looks at what happens with other choices.

Our candidate list, ordered by effect size:

```{r}
hits <- results %>%
  filter(dl_prob > 0.9, fdr < 0.1) %>%
  arrange(desc(RSS_diff)) %>%
  dplyr::select(protein, dl_prob, fdr, niche_control, niche_treated)

head(hits, 10)
```

And how do the previously reported movers score?

```{r}
results %>%
  filter(protein %in% known_movers) %>%
  dplyr::select(protein, dl_prob, fdr, niche_control, niche_treated)
```

:::{.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge 2: Choosing thresholds
{{< level 1 >}}

Thresholds are a choice, not a law of nature. Find how many candidates you
get if you use a more stringent threshold (DL probability > 0.95 and
FDR < 0.01) and a more exploratory one (DL probability > 0.8 and FDR < 0.2).
How many of the `known_movers` pass in each case?

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}

```{r}
stringent <- results %>% filter(dl_prob > 0.95, fdr < 0.01)
explore   <- results %>% filter(dl_prob > 0.8,  fdr < 0.2)

nrow(stringent)
nrow(explore)

sum(known_movers %in% stringent$protein)
sum(known_movers %in% explore$protein)
```

Loosening the thresholds recovers more of the known movers, at the cost of a
longer list that will contain more false positives. Which you choose depends
on what you will do next: a short list for expensive validation, or a longer
list for exploration and enrichment analysis.

:::
:::

## Where do the proteins move?

Because the marker-based test tells us the most probable niche in each
condition, we can summarise the movements of our candidates as a table of
*from* and *to* niches, similar to the `plotTable()` output of BANDLE.

```{r}
hits %>%
  dplyr::count(niche_control, niche_treated, sort = TRUE)
```

### Allowing for "unknown"

Notice that every protein in this table moves from one organelle to another.
There are no movements to or from `"unknown"`. This is not because no such
proteins exist, but because of how the niches are assigned. The marker-based
model is a mixture of the marker niches only: the niche probabilities of
every protein add up to 1 across the organelles, so the most probable niche is
*always* an organelle, even for a protein that sits between clusters and fits
none of them well. This is the same situation we met with the SVM in the
static lessons, where every protein was first assigned to a compartment and we
then applied a threshold to decide which assignments to trust.

We can do the same here. Note that this is not part of the SANDLE method
itself, which assigns each protein to its most probable niche
[@Crook2026]. It is an extra step we add to help describe the results.
`sandle_markers()` also returned the probability of
the most probable niche in each condition (`prob_control` and
`prob_treated`). Let's look at how these are distributed before choosing a
cutoff.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
results %>%
  dplyr::select(protein, prob_control, prob_treated) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-protein, names_to = "condition", values_to = "prob") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = prob)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ condition) +
  labs(x = "Probability of the most probable niche",
       y = "Number of proteins") +
  theme_bw()
```

Most proteins are assigned confidently, but a tail of proteins have no niche
with a high probability. We label a niche assignment as `"unknown"` when its
probability is below a cutoff. As with every threshold in this lesson, the
cutoff is a choice. Here we use 0.8.

```{r}
niche_cut <- 0.8

results <- results %>%
  mutate(loc_control = ifelse(prob_control >= niche_cut, niche_control, "unknown"),
         loc_treated = ifelse(prob_treated >= niche_cut, niche_treated, "unknown"))
```

This does not change the DL probability or the FDR of any protein, only how we
describe where a protein moves from and to.

:::{.callout-note}
#### Can a protein move to "unknown" and still have a high DL probability?
Yes. Consider a protein confidently assigned to the plasma membrane in the
basal condition, whose probability is split between the Golgi, endosomes and
lysosomes after insulin. Because almost none of its insulin probability is on
the plasma membrane, the DL probability is close to 1: the protein has very
probably left the plasma membrane. But no single destination is probable
enough to name, so it is best described as moving from the plasma membrane to
`"unknown"`. Without a cutoff, it would simply be reported as moving to
whichever niche happened to have the highest probability.
:::

### Types of movement

Proteins can change their profile in several ways, and the two tests respond
to them differently. To see this, we take all proteins that pass *either*
test and classify each by what happens to its niche assignment.

```{r}
candidates <- results %>%
  filter(dl_prob > 0.9 | fdr < 0.1) %>%
  mutate(
    test = case_when(dl_prob > 0.9 & fdr < 0.1 ~ "both",
                     dl_prob > 0.9             ~ "marker-based only",
                     TRUE                      ~ "marker-free only"),
    move = case_when(
      loc_control == "unknown" & loc_treated == "unknown" ~ "unknown -> unknown",
      loc_control == "unknown"                            ~ "unknown -> niche",
      loc_treated == "unknown"                            ~ "niche -> unknown",
      loc_control == loc_treated                          ~ "same niche",
      TRUE                                                ~ "niche -> niche"))

table(candidates$move, candidates$test)
```

Each type of movement tells us something different:

* **niche → niche**: the protein is confidently assigned to one organelle in
  each condition, and they differ. These are the clearest candidates.
* **niche → unknown** and **unknown → niche**: the protein leaves, or arrives
  at, a confidently assigned organelle, but its other location is uncertain.
  It may move to a compartment that is not represented in the markers, become
  distributed across several compartments, or sit between clusters.
* **unknown → unknown**: the profile changes, but the protein cannot be
  confidently assigned in either condition. These are proteins that sit
  between organelles or in more than one location.
* **same niche**: the profile changes significantly, but the protein is
  assigned to the same organelle in both conditions. These are mostly found by
  the marker-free test alone. They may reflect partial relocation, where only
  a fraction of the protein moves, a shift within a compartment, or a change
  that the markers cannot resolve. @Crook2026 interpret proteins with strong
  marker-free support but a low DL probability in the same way, as "more
  complex or heterogeneous spatial reorganisation rather than simple
  compartmental shifts".

Note that the marker-based test can flag movements of any of these types,
since the DL probability reflects any change in niche probabilities, not only
a change of the most probable niche. Our conservative list contained no
`"unknown"` simply because, until now, every protein was given its most
probable niche, however uncertain. The other types are often the
most biologically interesting, for example a protein recruited from the
cytosol to a membrane, but they need careful checking of the profiles.

We can now redo the *from*/*to* table for all candidates, with `"unknown"`
included.

```{r}
candidates %>%
  dplyr::count(loc_control, loc_treated, sort = TRUE)
```

:::{.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge 3: Proteins leaving the plasma membrane
{{< level 2 >}}

Using `results`, find all proteins that pass both thresholds and are
assigned to the plasma membrane in the basal condition. Where are they
assigned after insulin stimulation? Look back at the PCA plots and the
marker profiles: how well separated are the plasma membrane and the niches
they move to?

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}

```{r}
pm_leavers <- results %>%
  filter(dl_prob > 0.9, fdr < 0.1,
         niche_control == "Plasma membrane") %>%
  dplyr::select(protein, dl_prob, fdr, niche_control, niche_treated)

pm_leavers

pm_leavers %>% count(niche_treated)
```

Most of these candidates move from the plasma membrane niche to the Golgi
niche. In this dataset the plasma membrane and Golgi markers are close
together on the PCA plots and have similar profiles, so niche assignments
between them are less certain than between more distinct niches (you can
confirm this with `QSep()`, where the Golgi is the plasma membrane's closest
neighbour). This is a good example of why the niche labels should be
interpreted together with the data and the literature: the change in profile is
real (the marker-free test is significant), but "Golgi" may best be read as
"an intracellular membrane compartment near the Golgi". A niche label can only
be as specific as the markers that define it.

:::
:::

:::{.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge 4: How much does the niche cutoff matter?
{{< level 1 >}}

Repeat the classification of movement types with a looser (`niche_cut <- 0.5`)
and a stricter (`niche_cut <- 0.95`) cutoff. How does the number of movements
involving `"unknown"` change? Does the cutoff change which proteins are
candidates?

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}

```{r}
move_types <- function(res, cut) {
  res %>%
    filter(dl_prob > 0.9 | fdr < 0.1) %>%
    mutate(loc_control = ifelse(prob_control >= cut, niche_control, "unknown"),
           loc_treated = ifelse(prob_treated >= cut, niche_treated, "unknown"),
           move = case_when(
             loc_control == "unknown" & loc_treated == "unknown" ~ "unknown -> unknown",
             loc_control == "unknown"                            ~ "unknown -> niche",
             loc_treated == "unknown"                            ~ "niche -> unknown",
             loc_control == loc_treated                          ~ "same niche",
             TRUE                                                ~ "niche -> niche")) %>%
    dplyr::count(move)
}

move_types(results, 0.5)
move_types(results, 0.95)
```

A stricter cutoff labels more assignments as `"unknown"`, so more movements
involve `"unknown"` and fewer are niche → niche. The cutoff does not change
which proteins are candidates, because the candidates are chosen on the DL
probability and FDR only. It only changes how we describe their movement.

:::
:::

## Visualising the candidates

### Protein profiles

Always look at the data. `plot_protein_profiles()` plots the profiles of
chosen proteins in both conditions: thin lines are individual replicates,
thick lines the mean, and the shaded band ± 1 standard deviation.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = hits$protein[1:12],
                      labels = c("basal", "insulin"))
```

A convincing mover shows a consistent change in profile shape across all
three replicates, with little overlap between the two conditions.

Now let's look at two of the known movers. GLUT4 (P14142) is the classic
insulin-responsive protein, and Q8C129 is one of the strongest signals in this
dataset.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = c("P14142", "Q8C129"),
                      labels = c("basal", "insulin"))
```

Compare where each of these sits on the DL probability versus FDR plot above.
A protein can give a clear signal in one test and be borderline in the other,
which is why it helps to look at both.

We can also look at candidates that involve `"unknown"`. Here we plot the
strongest movers, by effect size, from each of the types that involve
`"unknown"`.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
unknown_movers <- candidates %>%
  filter(grepl("unknown", move)) %>%
  group_by(move) %>%
  slice_max(RSS_diff, n = 3) %>%
  ungroup()

unknown_movers %>%
  dplyr::select(protein, move, loc_control, loc_treated, dl_prob, fdr)

plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = unknown_movers$protein,
                      labels = c("basal", "insulin"))
```

### Movers on the spatial map

Finally, let's put a few movers back onto the PCA plots: the top four
candidates from both methods plus GLUT4 and Q8C129. We write one small function
that draws the PCA plot of a replicate and adds the movers on top. `plot2D()`
returns the PCA coordinates of every protein, which we use to place the
points. The `col` and `pch` arguments can be a single value (all movers look
the same) or one value per mover.

```{r}
movers <- c(hits$protein[1:4], "P14142", "Q8C129")

show_movers <- function(object, main, col = "yellow", pch = 21, labels = FALSE) {
  col <- setNames(rep(col, length.out = length(movers)), movers)
  pch <- setNames(rep(pch, length.out = length(movers)), movers)
  pca <- plot2D(object, fcol = "markers", main = main)  # returns PCA coordinates
  m <- movers[movers %in% rownames(pca)]
  points(pca[m, 1], pca[m, 2], pch = pch[m], bg = col[m], col = "black",
         cex = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  if (labels) text(pca[m, 1], pca[m, 2], m, pos = 3, cex = 0.7, font = 2)
}
```

First, all movers in yellow, labelled with their accession. The basal
replicates are on the top row and the insulin replicates on the bottom row.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:3) show_movers(control[[i]], paste("Basal, rep", i), labels = TRUE)
for (i in 1:3) show_movers(treated[[i]], paste("Insulin, rep", i), labels = TRUE)
```

It is easier to follow individual proteins if each has its own colour and
symbol.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
mover_col <- c("black", "red", "blue", "darkorange", "green3", "magenta")
mover_pch <- c(21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 21)

par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:3) show_movers(control[[i]], paste("Basal, rep", i), mover_col, mover_pch)
for (i in 1:3) show_movers(treated[[i]], paste("Insulin, rep", i), mover_col, mover_pch)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 1.5
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
legend("center", legend = movers, pch = mover_pch, pt.bg = mover_col,
       col = "black", pt.cex = 1.6, ncol = 3, bty = "n")
```

A mover should sit closer to a different organelle cluster after insulin
stimulation, and it should do so consistently across all three replicates.
A protein that moves to `"unknown"` will instead often move into the space
between clusters.

:::{.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge 5: Follow your own proteins
{{< level 2 >}}

Choose three proteins from Challenge 3, or from the movements involving
`"unknown"` above. Plot their profiles with `plot_protein_profiles()` and show
them on the PCA plots using `show_movers()`. Remember that `show_movers()` uses
the `movers` object, so you will need to redefine it first.

::: {.callout-answer collapse=true}

```{r}
## Here we take the top protein of each movement type involving "unknown"
movers <- unknown_movers %>%
  group_by(move) %>%
  slice_max(RSS_diff, n = 1) %>%
  pull(protein)
movers

plot_protein_profiles(control, treated, proteins = movers,
                      labels = c("basal", "insulin"))

par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:3) show_movers(control[[i]], paste("Basal, rep", i),
                           col = c("black", "brown", "yellow"), pch = 21:23)
for (i in 1:3) show_movers(treated[[i]], paste("Insulin, rep", i),
                           col = c("black", "brown", "yellow"), pch = 21:23)
```

:::
:::

### Visualising overall trends

There are several different ways we can visualise the overall movement trend
of these proteins. The `bandle` package has functions to generate alluvial
(also known as Sankey) and chord (also known as circos) plots to capture the
flow of proteins between conditions.

Let's load the `bandle` package.

```{r}
library("bandle")
```

The `plotTranslocations` function takes a list of two `MSnSet`s, one per
condition, and a feature data column giving the localisation of each protein
in each condition. We subset replicate 1 of each condition to our candidates
(here all proteins passing either test), and add the niche assignments,
including `"unknown"`, as a new feature data column called `sandle.pred`.

```{r}
## Extract candidates from both conditions
msnset_cands <- list(control[[1]][candidates$protein, ],
                     treated[[1]][candidates$protein, ])

## Add the niche assignments in each condition
fData(msnset_cands[[1]])$sandle.pred <- candidates$loc_control
fData(msnset_cands[[2]])$sandle.pred <- candidates$loc_treated

## Check the number of proteins in each object
lapply(msnset_cands, nrow)
```

If we examine this new object `msnset_cands` we see it is a `list` containing
replicate 1 of the basal data and replicate 1 of the insulin data
respectively, subsetted for just the `r nrow(candidates)` proteins which are
differential localisation candidates.

Next, we set a colour scheme for the subcellular classes, with `"unknown"` in
grey, and pass `msnset_cands` to `plotTranslocations`, specifying the `fcol`
containing our niche assignments. The default plot generated by
`plotTranslocations` is an alluvial plot, which uses code from the
`ggalluvial` R package.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
## Set the colours of the plot to match the organelles
mrkCl <- getMarkerClasses(control[[1]], fcol = "markers")
cols <- c(getStockcol()[seq(mrkCl)], "grey")
names(cols) <- c(mrkCl, "unknown")

## Plot the flow of proteins
alluvial <- plotTranslocations(params = msnset_cands,
                               fcol = "sandle.pred",
                               col = cols)
alluvial + ggtitle("Differential localisation: basal to insulin")
```

The same information can be shown as a chord diagram by setting
`type = "chord"`.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
plotTranslocations(params = msnset_cands,
                   fcol = "sandle.pred",
                   col = cols,
                   type = "chord")
```

Proteins that stay in the same niche are included in these plots, as flows
from a niche to itself. To show only proteins whose niche assignment changes,
subset `candidates` with `filter(loc_control != loc_treated)` before building
`msnset_cands`.


## Interpreting the results

Computational prediction of differential localisation is largely
**exploratory**. LOPIT data contains noise between fractions and replicates,
and some proteins naturally sit between organelles or in several at once. The
results should be used as a starting point for further investigation (for
example, searching the literature for evidence of movement, imaging, or
biochemical follow-up), rather than as validation in themselves.

Some things to keep in mind:

* **Markers are assumed not to move.** If a marker protein does relocate, the
  marker-based test cannot detect it, and it may distort the niche model. The
  marker-free test does not have this limitation.
* **Niche assignments are always to a marker niche.** The marker-based model
  only knows about the niches defined by the markers, so the most probable
  niche is always one of them. Thresholding the niche probability lets us
  describe uncertain assignments as `"unknown"`, and reveals movements to and
  from compartments that are not well represented by the markers.
* **Results depend on data quality.** Poorly resolved niches lead to uncertain
  assignments, which in turn inflate DL probabilities. Always check
  resolution first.
* **The marker-based test has a random component.** The robust fitting step
  uses random subsampling, particularly for niches with few markers. Set a
  seed for reproducibility, and treat proteins close to a threshold with
  caution.
* **Thresholds are your choice.** Requiring both a high DL probability and a
  low FDR gives a short list supported by two kinds of evidence. Using either
  test, or looser thresholds, gives a longer list for exploration, including
  movements to and from `"unknown"` and changes within a niche. Choose based
  on your question and how you will follow up the candidates.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

* A protein is **differentially localised** if it changes subcellular niche
  between conditions, seen as a change in the *shape* of its profile across
  fractions.
* **SANDLE** detects differential localisation in seconds, with no priors,
  MCMC or HPC, making it a fast and robust alternative to BANDLE.
* The **marker-based** test models each niche with a robust *t*-distribution
  and gives a **DL probability**, together with the most likely niche in each
  condition.
* The **marker-free** test compares profiles between conditions and gives
  a **p-value and FDR** without needing any markers.
* The most likely niche is always one of the marker niches. Thresholding its
  probability labels uncertain assignments as `"unknown"`, revealing
  movements to and from `"unknown"` as well as between organelles.
* How to threshold, and on which test, is up to you: stringent for a short
  list, looser for exploration. Candidates should always be checked by
  plotting profiles and spatial maps, and followed up experimentally.
:::
